title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
authors: Jiyuan Wang, Qian Zhang, Guoqing Harry Xu, Miryung Kim
abstract: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy

infographic.key_insight: QDIFF tests quantum software stacks by comparing output distributions across semantically equivalent program variants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It targets correctness across quantum languages, compilers, simulators, and hardware execution while reducing costly hardware tests.
method: Generate program variants using semantics-preserving source-to-source transformations.
Filter circuits before hardware execution using depth, two-qubit operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time.
Check distribution equivalence using extensible comparisons such as Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests and cross entropy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the testing approach but reports no benchmark sizes, bug counts, or measured speedups.
infographic.watch_item: Statistical comparisons must account for sampling variability and hardware noise to avoid flagging expected variation as software defects.
infographic.paper_title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks

title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts
authors: Dmytro Sapozhnyk
abstract: Max-Cut is a common testbed for near-term quantum optimization because it has a simple Ising Hamiltonian, established classical baselines, and a parameterized quantum circuit whose performance depends on the outer classical optimizer. This paper develops QASPA-MaxCut, a shift-phase circuit for Max-Cut that encodes graph edges through controlled $R_y$ rotations of the form $\mathrm{CX}_{ij}R_y(θ_{ij})\mathrm{CX}_{ij}$. We derive the exact two-qubit algebra of the edge block, trace an unweighted four-vertex example, and compare one-layer QASPA-MaxCut with depth-one QAOA by exact state-vector simulation. The protocol uses seed 42, evaluates connected backbone-augmented random graphs with additional-edge probabilities $p_{\mathrm{edge}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, and adds nineteen custom unweighted topologies. The QASPA-MaxCut score is reported after the algorithm's classical selection stage: the four leading QASPA bit strings are evaluated by the Max-Cut objective, and the best cut is retained. The QAOA score is the expected approximation ratio after local optimization, reported as a best-of-$k$ curve over one to ten restarts. In these small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut produces reported group-mean selection ratios between $0.955$ and $1.000$, the topology-level readout is unchanged in the retained finite-shot checks under the rule $\lceil 0.03047\cdot 2^n+1016.2\rceil$, and depth-one QAOA improves with additional classical restarts while remaining lower than the QASPA selection score in the reported mean summaries. This comparison motivates further study of the classical search budget needed to obtain competitive Max-Cut samples at shallow circuit depth.

infographic.key_insight: In small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut achieves mean selection ratios of 0.955–1.000, exceeding the reported depth-one QAOA mean expected ratios.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results motivate testing whether shallow edge-encoding circuits can reduce classical optimization effort for Max-Cut.
method: Encode graph edges with CX–Ry(θ)–CX blocks in a shift-phase circuit.
Evaluate the four leading QASPA bit strings classically and retain the best cut.
Compare against depth-one QAOA with one to ten classical optimization restarts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Seed-42 exact state-vector tests cover backbone-augmented random graphs at four additional-edge probabilities and 19 custom unweighted topologies; retained finite-shot checks preserve topology-level readouts under the stated shot rule.
infographic.watch_item: QASPA’s best-of-four selection score and QAOA’s expected ratio are different metrics, so these small simulations do not establish an equal-budget or hardware advantage.
infographic.paper_title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts

title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing
authors: Pim van den Heuvel, Vrinda Mehta, Dennis Willsch, J. A. Montanez-Barrera, Kristel Michielsen
abstract: Quantum computing has emerged as a new tool for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Quantum optimization approaches usually operate on the subclass of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. Many optimization problems can be reformulated in this form, though there are often multiple ways to do so. The choice of formulation can considerably affect the performance of QUBO solvers in practice. In this work, we study QUBO formulations of the Knapsack problem, a canonical example of a problem with inequality constraints. In the standard formulation these constraints are converted into penalty terms, which requires additional slack variables. Here, we investigate three more resource-efficient approaches for formulating the Knapsack as a QUBO. The first two modify the standard formulation, either by deriving a smaller penalty constant or by reducing the number of slack variables. The third approach is a wholly different method, which avoids the use of slack variables entirely. All three approaches increase the probability of finding the optimal solution, both in simulations of the linear ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) and on a D-Wave quantum annealer. The slackless method performs best, increasing success probabilities by several orders of magnitude even for relatively small problem sizes.

infographic.key_insight: Resource-efficient Knapsack QUBO formulations improve optimal-solution success, with a slackless formulation delivering gains of several orders of magnitude in the reported tests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing a better QUBO formulation can reduce auxiliary-variable overhead or penalty strength while improving quantum optimization performance.
method: Derive a smaller penalty constant for the standard formulation.
Reduce the number of slack variables used to encode capacity constraints.
Use an alternative formulation that eliminates slack variables entirely.
infographic.evidence_signal: All three approaches increased optimal-solution probabilities in LR-QAOA simulations and on a D-Wave quantum annealer; the slackless method performed best.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish scaling to large instances or an advantage over classical optimization methods.
infographic.paper_title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing

title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
authors: Aldana Al-Sulaiti, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir, Ahmed Farouk, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum knowledge distillation enables transfer across quantum and classical models, but reported benefits depend on the task and architecture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Distillation may support model compression, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment using quantum-derived supervision.
method: Classify approaches by teacher–student configuration and the role of quantum resources.
Distinguish quantum-inspired methods from classical quantum simulation and quantum-hardware execution.

title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
authors: Tong Jiang, Andrew Zhao, Shashwat Kumar, Jigyasa Nigam, Eliott Rosenberg, Ryan Babbush
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learning models compress quantum measurement data to rapidly supply wavefunction overlaps, accelerating quantum-classical Monte Carlo by orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reusing learned quantum-state information reduces classical processing costs that constrain hybrid quantum simulation workflows.
method: Prepare trial wavefunctions on a quantum processor to guide classical quantum Monte Carlo.
Compress quantum measurement data into machine-learning models.

infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify training costs or how overlap-prediction errors affect accuracy beyond the demonstrated systems.
infographic.paper_title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo

title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
authors: Junkai Zeng, Hao Liang, Yong-Ju Hai, Xiu-Hao Deng
abstract: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.

infographic.key_insight: Deterministically optimized twirling sequences shape coherent-error trajectories to keep accumulated error bounded at O(1), versus O(√N) scaling for randomized compiling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects pulse-level robust control with circuit compilation to suppress coherent errors without logical encoding or ancillary qubits.
method: Map coherent-error accumulation in digital circuits to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space.
Optimize twirling sequences deterministically to cancel error contributions through destructive interference.
Combine circuit-level trajectory shaping with pulse-level robust control.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports bounded O(1) error scaling and synergy with robust pulses, but provides no numerical benchmarks or hardware-validation details.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on coherent-noise characterization and the errors introduced by additional twirling gates.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression

title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
authors: Ke-Xin Tang, Zhen-Qiang Weng, Kai Yan, Yao-Yao Lu, Yu-Ze Zhu, Hang Song
abstract: Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

infographic.key_insight: DiffSequence-Q uses quantum auxiliary supervision during training to guide protein diffusion design toward secondary structure requirements and solubility targets, while generation remains entirely classical.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The hybrid approach allows quantum models to influence protein design without requiring quantum computation during sequence generation.
method: Condition multinomial diffusion on per-residue secondary structure and a continuous solubility target.
Jointly train a shared Transformer with diffusion loss and an auxiliary solubility prediction loss from a QNN or QKAN.
Generate protein sequences through classical reverse diffusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: On CATH, DiffSequence-Q led four evaluated models in complete-generation secondary structure recovery; the best QNN and QKAN configurations scored 14.0% and 22.7% above the MLP baseline in mean predicted solubility, and selected proteins showed antifungal or enzymatic activity experimentally.
infographic.watch_item: Solubility improvements were assessed by a separate prediction model; the abstract does not establish measured solubility gains or practical quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling
authors: Raul Martinez, Miguel Sánchez-Beato, Matilde Osa, Jorge Parra, Mario Calonge
abstract: Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.

infographic.key_insight: For the scheduling instance and initialization studied, an entanglement-free VQA produced feasible schedules without gains from entangling circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Day-by-day decomposition and logarithmic binary encoding kept scheduling batches within 30 qubits while accounting for worker capacities, skills, priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability.
method: Formulate multi-skill project scheduling as a QUBO and propagate remaining workload between daily batches.
Compare linear and brick-wall entangling ansätze with an entanglement-free reference using equal parameter counts.
Train each configuration with COBYLA and Adam using SPSA gradient estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulation, the entanglement-free reference yielded feasible schedules with both optimizers; with COBYLA, it came closest to the required workload at a fraction of the entangled circuits’ simulation cost.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the instance and initialization studied; broader performance and robustness on noisy quantum hardware remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling

title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization
authors: Eunjin In, Kristina D. Launey, Darin C. Mumma, James A. Sauls
abstract: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert-Schmidt asymmetry $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$, which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit $S$-wave $p+{}^3\mathrm{He}$ two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from $\textit{ab initio}$ many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, $\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{HS}$-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Hilbert–Schmidt asymmetry can guide variational quantum optimization toward a target symmetry sector without requiring symmetry-preserving preparation circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Symmetry-based guidance offers a way to improve VQE accuracy and reliability while retaining flexibility in circuit design.
method: Quantify deviations from symmetry using quantum-accessible Hilbert–Schmidt asymmetry.
Use the asymmetry objective to guide optimization toward collective SU(2) singlet states.
Benchmark against direct energy minimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Proof-of-principle tests on a five-qubit nuclear two-cluster Hamiltonian and collective spin models with up to 12 particles increased singlet probability and improved energy accuracy and ground-state fidelity, with substantial fidelity gains in larger spin systems.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish measurement overhead, noise robustness, or scalability beyond the tested systems.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization

title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
authors: Afonso Azenha, Ilia Polian, Sebastian Brandhofer
abstract: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum interaction graph (QIG) transpilation method lowers routing costs and scales to distributed superconducting quantum architectures with restricted connectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-aware mapping and routing can make compilation more practical for multi-QPU systems without assuming ideal connectivity.
method: Represent circuit interactions using a quantum interaction graph.
Partition the graph to map computations across QPUs.
Apply a fast SABRE-inspired heuristic to route under inter- and intra-module connectivity constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a 48-qubit system, QIG reduced average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% and delivered over 250× speed-ups for structured workloads versus DMapS; on 399-qubit IBM Flamingo, it maintained practical runtimes and cut structured routing costs by up to 51.96% versus DQC-adapted SABRE.
infographic.watch_item: Reported gains depend on workload, topology, and baseline; the abstract does not establish execution-fidelity improvements on physical hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures

title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls
authors: Eduardo Willwock Lussi, Rafael de Santiago, Eduardo Inacio Duzzioni, Hector Bessa Silveira
abstract: High-fidelity quantum gates are a central requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet their implementation is limited by the sensitivity of qubits to environmental noise and by control non-idealities. To mitigate these effects, quantum gates can be designed as dynamically corrected gates (DCGs), where control sequences are engineered to suppress the impact of errors on the resulting operation. Many methods in the literature are able to synthesize DCGs, but they typically rely on numerical optimization, with synthesis times on the order of minutes per gate. Here, we propose an automated semi-analytical method that reduces this cost by orders of magnitude, synthesizing smooth, robust control pulses in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness. Our approach is based on the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, where quantum evolution is mapped onto a geometric space curve whose geometric properties determine the target gate and its robustness. We parameterize the curve in the Frenet-Serret frame and employ the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) to design controls that are robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. The PMP is formulated as a boundary-value problem and solved using a shooting method. The Frenet-Serret frame is integrated using Rodrigues' formula. Starting from a reference solution, we gradually vary the target rotation angle to construct a library of solutions, whose interpolation provides initial guesses for the shooting parameters of new target gates. We evaluated the method on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, obtaining a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparation of the interpolation base. Quantum propagation yielded nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.

infographic.key_insight: A semi-analytical geometric method synthesizes robust single-qubit controls in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster pulse synthesis could reduce control-design overhead for quantum hardware while suppressing sensitivity to amplitude and dephasing errors.
method: Map quantum evolution to space curves using Space Curve Quantum Control and Frenet–Serret geometry.
Apply the Pontryagin Maximum Principle and solve the resulting boundary-value problem by shooting.

infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,000 single-qubit rotations, mean local optimization took 39.945 ms per gate after interpolation-base preparation; quantum propagation gave nominal infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction and verified robustness to quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.
infographic.watch_item: The reported timing excludes interpolation-base preparation, and the abstract does not establish experimental hardware performance or robustness to time-varying noise.
infographic.paper_title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls

title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
authors: Ke-Sean J. M. Peter, Ryan A. Kowalski, David A. Curie, Dakota Braaten, Matthew W. Day, Denis R. Candido
abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

infographic.key_insight: Boron nitride nanotubes host multiple room-temperature single-photon emitters at different visible wavelengths within a compact, approximately 25 nm radius.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These nanotubes offer a potential platform for compact multiwavelength quantum light sources integrated with waveguides and interferometric filters.
method: Locate and characterize emitters using confocal photoluminescence microscopy.
Assess single-photon emission using Hanbury Brown–Twiss interferometry.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports emitters spanning the visible spectrum, multiple emission wavelengths along individual tubes, lifetimes as short as 0.5 ns, and improved stability after surface treatment.
infographic.watch_item: Deterministic placement and photonic-circuit integration remain prospective; the abstract provides no quantitative photon-purity or long-term stability metrics.
infographic.paper_title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes

title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication
authors: Chandrima Kayal, Rajat Mittal, Manaswi Paraashar, Nitin Saurabh
abstract: In the world of quantum computing, quantum Fourier transform (QFT) has been one of the most important subroutines for quantum algorithms, as exemplified by Shor's factoring algorithms and phase estimation (which in itself has been used as a primitive in various quantum algorithms). In fact most of the well known quantum algorithms can be divided into two classes, QFT based algorithms and search based algorithms. The usual circuit for QFT (covered in almost every basic quantum algorithms course) needs $O(q^2)$ gates (and $O(q)$ qubits) to perform the exact Fourier transform over $\mathbb{F}_{2^q}$. Cleve and Watrous (FOCS 2000) improved this gate count to $O(q (\log q)^2 (\log \log q))$ using the integer multiplication algorithm in $O(n (\log n) (\log \log n))$ time for two $n$-bit integers (best known at that time). Our first main result shows that this gate count can be improved to $O(q (\log q))$. In fact, if there is a multiplication circuit, to multiply two $n$-bit integers, with $O(n (\log n)^α)$ gates; we get a QFT circuit with $O(q (\log q)^α)$ gates (improving upon $O(q (\log q)^{α+ 1})$) gates from the construction of Cleve and Watrous). Given the recent claim by OpenAI about integer multiplication, this opens up the possibility of having a QFT circuit with $o \left( q (\log q)\right)$ gates. On approximating the QFT over $\ZZ/(2^q \ZZ)$, the result of Ahokas, Cleve and Hales (ERATO 2003) showed that an approximating circuit can be built with $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^{α+1} \right)$ gates, where $ε$ is the approximating parameter. Our second main result again improves this to $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^α \right)$ gates.

infographic.key_insight: A tighter reduction from integer multiplication to the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) removes one logarithmic factor from prior exact and approximate QFT gate bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower QFT gate counts could reduce the resources needed for phase estimation and Shor-type algorithms.
method: Convert an O(n(log n)^α)-gate multiplication circuit into an O(q(log q)^α)-gate exact QFT circuit.
Obtain an O(q log q) exact QFT gate bound.
Reduce the approximate QFT bound to O(q(log log(q/ε))^α), where ε controls approximation error.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical circuit-complexity improvements over prior constructions, not hardware experiments or empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Asymptotic gate savings do not establish practical hardware speedups, and the suggested sub-O(q log q) possibility is conditional on improved multiplication circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
authors: Yuya Kawamata, Keisuke Fujii
abstract: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Neural surrogates trained on quantum-hardware samples accelerated autocorrelation decay in constrained Boltzmann sampling with more than 1,000 binary variables.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A divide-and-conquer implementation extends quantum-assisted sampling to large systems by using neural surrogates for quantum-generated proposals.
method: Generate QAOA training samples on an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor.
Train neural surrogates for quantum-enhanced MCMC.
Use divide-and-conquer subproblems to support larger systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments covered N=144 and N=1064; at N=1064, autocorrelation decay per MCMC step was approximately 5.2× and 12.3× faster than global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Larger subproblems challenged neural-surrogate learning, and faster decay per MCMC step does not establish an end-to-end runtime advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling

title: Bounded decoding complexity in transversal circuits with magic state injection
authors: Lukas M. Sieberer, Giacomo Giudice
abstract: We characterize the complexity of space-time correlated decoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures that implement Clifford gates transversally and realize non-Clifford gates via magic state injection. In this approach, decoding graphs for logical measurements are constructed by backpropagating measurement operators through the circuit, which causes them to grow with circuit volume. However, the decoding volume can be substantially reduced by decoding measurements sequentially, committing corrections, and excluding syndrome data that have already been processed for earlier measurements. For random circuits, we find that the resulting decoding volume associated with mid-circuit measurements approaches a stationary average that is determined by the density of magic state injections. Large decoding instances are exponentially suppressed. We further find that the decoding complexity is remarkably insensitive to different choices of measurement products to be decoded, and that the same qualitative behavior persists across different circuit connectivities and Clifford gate ensembles. These results suggest that scalable space-time correlated decoding of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum algorithms is achievable since the magic states that make transversal architectures universal also keep them decodable.

infographic.key_insight: Magic state injections enable universal computation in transversal architectures while keeping sequential decoding volumes statistically bounded in the random circuits studied.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sequential decoding could make space-time correlated error correction scalable by preventing decoding instances from growing with total circuit volume.
method: Backpropagate logical measurement operators to construct space-time decoding graphs.
Decode measurements sequentially, commit corrections, and exclude previously processed syndrome data.
Compare decoding volumes across measurement-product choices, circuit connectivities, and Clifford gate ensembles.
infographic.evidence_signal: For random circuits, mid-circuit decoding volumes approach a stationary average set by magic state injection density, with large instances exponentially suppressed and similar qualitative behavior across tested circuit variants.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish end-to-end decoder runtime or real-time performance for structured, application-scale algorithms.
infographic.paper_title: Bounded decoding complexity in transversal circuits with magic state injection

title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
authors: Bin Cheng, Naixu Guo, Feng Pan
abstract: Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.

infographic.key_insight: Exact certification reveals that some reported quantum code and circuit distances are overstated, changing reliability estimates and design choices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certified distances help engineers compare codes, optimize error-correction schedules, and retain defective hardware that still meets protection targets.
method: Express code and circuit distances as tropical partition functions.
Evaluate using rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search, aided by reductions and relaxations.
Certify exact distances by matching proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors certify codes with up to 31,200 qubits and circuits with up to 800,000 fault mechanisms; an audit finds distance discrepancies in 10 of 26 papers.
infographic.watch_item: Schedule improvements can add overhead: restoring IBM two-gross circuit distance from 16 to 18 at one noisy cycle requires an extra timestep per cycle.
infographic.paper_title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale

title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
authors: Nuno Batista, Gabriel Falcao, Penousal Machado
abstract: Choosing a quantum error-correcting code for a real device means scoring candidates with circuit-level simulations so slow that only a few hundred can be run. So every evaluation counts, and a search is judged by how many good codes it finds per paid evaluation. Quantum LDPC codes built from a few group elements protect many logical qubits, but good ones are rare in a huge space. We introduce GFlowQEC, to our knowledge the first generative flow network (GFlowNet) for quantum code design. It builds a code one group element at a time and learns to propose codes in proportion to a power of their score. We train it once on scores from earlier searches, freeze it, and let it propose lifted-product codes with 180 physical qubits, scored by their distances. Ranking ten of its draws per paid call, it finds more than twice as many new top-scoring codes (inequivalent to any it was trained on) as tuned parallel tempering, even when tempering starts from GFlowQEC's training codes. It finds more than three and a half times as many as a supervised screen ranking ten random candidates per call. When both rank a hundred, the screen beats GFlowQEC, and does best ranking GFlowQEC's draws. Soft Q-learning, which shares the GFlowNet's optimal policy, does as well at one noise bias and better at the other, so the gain does not depend on the GFlowNet's training loss. Trained proposers can make a budget of expensive evaluations go further when good codes are rare.

infographic.key_insight: A pretrained generative proposer can find more high-scoring quantum LDPC codes per expensive evaluation than tuned search baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning from previous code evaluations can stretch limited search budgets when strong quantum error-correcting codes are rare.
method: Construct lifted-product codes one group element at a time with a GFlowNet.
Train on earlier search scores to sample codes in proportion to a power of their score, then freeze the model.
Rank batches of generated candidates before paying to evaluate selected codes.
infographic.evidence_signal: For distance-scored codes with 180 physical qubits, ranking 10 draws per paid evaluation found over twice as many new, training-inequivalent top-scoring codes as tuned parallel tempering and over 3.5 times as many as a supervised screen ranking 10 random candidates.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage depends on the comparison: the supervised screen won at batch size 100, and soft Q-learning matched or exceeded GFlowQEC across the two tested noise biases.
infographic.paper_title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes

title: Classical training of conditional instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machines
authors: Oriol Balló-Gimbernat, Emiliano Tolotti, Laia Domingo, Fernando Vilariño, Adan Garriga
abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) Born machines are attractive quantum generative models, as certain IQP circuit families are conjectured to be hard to sample, yet they can be trained classically. Previously proposed conditional IQP Born machines make the parameters of the diagonal layer condition dependent. We introduce conditional IQP Born machines, in which the condition is encoded in the input state and a single IQP unitary is shared across conditions. Efficient sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation for the reference state entering the diagonal layer suffice to obtain unbiased classical estimates of a conditional maximum mean discrepancy objective and its gradients. We show that input conditioning can represent conditional families that no diagonally conditioned IQP model with the same number of qubits can reproduce. For the sixteen-qubit Curie-Weiss spin model, a single conditional model captures the magnetization transition at held-out temperatures. Its mean total variation distance is six times lower than that of diagonal conditioning under the same protocol and comparable to that of classical generative models with up to seven times as many parameters. We also train conditional models classically with up to 2048 qubits, which reproduce the mean squared magnetization of the target away from the crossover. These results extend classically trained IQP Born machines to conditional generation.

infographic.key_insight: Encoding conditions in the input state lets one shared IQP circuit represent conditional distributions beyond those achievable by diagonal conditioning with the same qubit count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables classical training of conditional quantum generative models while sharing circuit parameters across conditions.
method: Encode each condition in the input state rather than in diagonal-layer parameters.
Apply a single shared IQP unitary across conditions.
Use efficient reference-state sampling and amplitude ratios to estimate conditional maximum mean discrepancy and gradients without bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 16-qubit Curie–Weiss model, mean total variation distance was six times lower than diagonal conditioning at held-out temperatures; models up to 2048 qubits reproduced mean squared magnetization away from the crossover.
infographic.watch_item: Classical training requires efficient reference-state sampling and amplitude-ratio evaluation; large-scale moment agreement alone does not establish full-distribution accuracy or quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Classical training of conditional instantaneous quantum polynomial-time Born machines

title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
authors: Long Huang
abstract: Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

infographic.key_insight: With a fixed measurement basis, gate-optimal repetition-code tomography requires only 0, 1 and 5 recovery gates for 3, 5 and 7 qubits, respectively, and more correction is not always better.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing recovery rather than defaulting to minimum-weight decoding can reduce gate overhead and improve tomography precision on superconducting hardware.
method: Exhaustively enumerate recovery designs for 3-, 5- and 7-qubit repetition codes.
Determine rank using exact modular arithmetic at two primes.
Evaluate precision under a calibration-residual floor across sampled working points.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 40 sampled working points, the three-gate 3-qubit design was more precise than the standard six-gate decoder every time, with a median improvement of 9.5× and a range of 1.8–88×.
infographic.watch_item: Low recovery-gate counts do not guarantee practical tomography: conditioning keeps designs with 5 or more qubits out of reach in the reported analysis.
infographic.paper_title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits

title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
authors: Angela Sara Cacciapuoti, Jessica Illiano, Caterina De Risi, Marcello Caleffi
abstract: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum networks can use coherence and shared entanglement to shape network functions, not merely transport quantum states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement may need to account for evolving entanglement and operational relationships beyond physical links.
method: Treat entanglement as a distributed, stateful resource whose changing condition remains visible to network functions.
Explore entanglement generation through coherent spatial-path superposition and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement.
Propose Quantum Addressing to represent these relationships alongside classical addressing and signaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual Perspective with two illustrative mechanisms, but reports no quantitative benchmarks or experimental evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Practical designs must track decohering entanglement and coordinate quantum-aware functions with classical signaling; implementation overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
